name: THE WHAT'S THE MATTER-HORN BURGER (with Swiss cheese crisps)

recipe.history: Swiss cheese — specifically the family of cheeses produced in Switzerland using the alpine milk of cows pastured in high-altitude meadows — has one of the most distinctive and well-documented cheesemaking histories in the world. Emmental, the canonical Swiss cheese with its trademark large round holes, has been produced in the Emme Valley of the canton of Bern for centuries, with written records of its trade appearing as early as 1293. The holes — called eyes by cheesemakers — are produced by Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria, which during the warm-room aging phase consume lactic acid and release carbon dioxide, forming bubbles that become the characteristic voids in the paste. Swiss alpine cheesemaking, including Gruyère, Appenzeller, and Raclette alongside Emmental, developed as a way to preserve the extraordinary summer milk of high-altitude dairy herds — milk produced by cows grazing on the botanical diversity of alpine meadows, which gives Swiss cheese its signature complexity: nutty, sweet, slightly fruity, with a long finish and none of the sharp, aggressive qualities of aged cheddar or the pungency of washed-rind cheeses. Gruyère specifically, produced in the canton of Fribourg, is perhaps the most sophisticated of the Swiss family — it melts with exceptional smoothness, it ages with remarkable depth and complexity, and its flavor profile, built on notes of hazelnuts, brown butter, dried fruit, and a long, sweet-savory finish, is among the most complex of any cow's milk cheese in the world.
recipe.history2: Swiss cheese arrived in the American consciousness primarily through mass-produced Emmental-style cheese, standardized and mild, that became a fixture of deli sandwiches and cheese plates from the mid-twentieth century onward. But the technique of baking or frying cheese into crisps — thin, lacey wafers of pure caramelized cheese with crisp edges and concentrated flavor — belongs to a different tradition, one rooted in both Swiss and Italian cooking. Frico, the Friulian Italian cheese crisp made from Montasio, is perhaps the most famous example; the Swiss equivalent is found in rösti preparations and fondue accompaniments. The cheese crisp as a burger topping represents the craft burger movement of the 2000s and 2010s at its most inventive: rather than simply melting cheese over the patty in the conventional way, baking thin rounds of Gruyère or Emmental into rigid, crackling wafers and stacking them on top creates a structural and textural element that is entirely new — the cheese is simultaneously a topping, a crunch element, and a concentrated flavor delivery system, all in a single thin disc of golden, caramelized dairy.
recipe.history3_personal: I made my first cheese crisp out of desperation. I was making fondue for a dinner party and had grated far more Gruyère than I needed, and rather than let it go to waste I scattered it in thin rounds on a parchment-lined baking sheet and put it in the oven at low heat while I was finishing other things. When I pulled the sheet out twenty minutes later, the cheese had melted, spread, bubbled, and then set into thin, golden, fragrant lacey rounds that were already starting to crisp at the edges. I had intended to snack on them privately but one of my guests walked into the kitchen at that exact moment and the entire batch was consumed standing at the counter before anything else was served. The fondue was fine. The cheese crisps were the best thing I made that evening. I have since concluded that the best possible use of Gruyère — better than fondue, better than gratins, better than even the classic croque monsieur — is this direct, unmediated transformation of the cheese itself into a crisp, concentrated, shattering wafer of pure flavor. And putting that wafer on a hamburger is, without question, the correct thing to do with it.
recipe.history4_philosophy: The Swiss cheese crisp on this burger is a lesson in what happens when you commit fully to an ingredient — when you take Gruyère not as a melting agent applied to a patty but as a primary flavor element that demands to be experienced in its most concentrated form. That commitment, however, only works in service of a patty that is itself handled with the same respect. Medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is the temperature at which the beef patty is most fully itself: juicy, fat-enriched, pink, yielding, carrying the deep Maillard-browned crust on its exterior and the soft, mineral-rich interior that is the entire argument for eating beef in this form. The cheese crisp's concentrated nuttiness, its slight caramelized bitterness, its structural crunch — all of these qualities are in dialogue with the patty's richness and yield. A well-done patty is dry and dense, and the cheese crisp's contrast of crunch and caramelized fat becomes less interesting against it, less alive. At medium rare, every element has its opposite: soft against crisp, pink against golden-brown, yielding against shattering. That is the burger. That is what it is supposed to be.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
280g Gruyère cheese, finely grated (or a blend of Gruyère and Emmental)
Salt and white pepper to taste
2 tbsp dry white wine or apple cider
4 thin slices Gruyère (for melting directly on the patty)
instructions: 1. Make the caramelized onions (can be done up to 3 days ahead): Melt butter with olive oil in a large, wide skillet or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add all sliced onions and salt. Cook, stirring every 5 minutes, for 45–60 minutes, until the onions are deeply golden brown, sweet, and jammy. If the onions start to stick, add a splash of water or wine. In the final 10 minutes, add sugar, white wine, and fresh thyme. Cook until the liquid is absorbed. The finished onions should be a deep caramel brown with a jam-like consistency. Cool and refrigerate if making ahead.

2. Make the Swiss cheese crisps: Preheat oven to 375°F / 190°C. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone baking mats. Arrange grated Gruyère in 4 thin rounds on the parchment, each about 4–5 inches in diameter, using about 50–60g of cheese per crisp. Spread the cheese evenly — the rounds should be thin and lacey. Sprinkle a little black pepper and caraway seed over each if using. Bake for 8–11 minutes, watching closely, until the crisps are evenly golden, lacy, and bubbling. Remove from oven and let cool completely on the parchment without moving them — they will crisp up as they cool. They should be rigid and shattering when tapped. If they remain pliable, return to the oven for 2–3 minutes.

3. Make the whole-grain mustard cream: Whisk together crème fraîche, whole-grain Dijon, regular Dijon, honey, and apple cider vinegar until smooth. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix on low 2 minutes, then medium 4 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Mix on medium-high 6–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Rise in a covered, oiled bowl 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

5. Divide bun dough into 4 portions, shape into balls, flatten onto a parchment-lined baking sheet. Proof covered 45–60 minutes. Brush with egg wash and bake at 375°F / 190°C for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

6. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 225g each). Form into round patties 3/4 inch thick. Press a dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and onion powder just before cooking.
7. Cook the patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat for 3 minutes until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place patties in the skillet. Cook undisturbed 3 minutes.

8. Flip once. Place a thin slice of Gruyère on each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes, covering the pan in the last minute to melt the cheese. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare. Remove from heat and rest 3–4 minutes on a wire rack.
9. Warm the caramelized onions: If made ahead, gently rewarm the caramelized onions in a small skillet over medium-low heat until heated through, 3–4 minutes.
10. Toast the buns: Slice buns and toast cut-side down in a lightly buttered skillet over medium heat until golden, 1–2 minutes.

11. Assemble: Spread whole-grain mustard cream generously on both bun halves. Add a handful of watercress or arugula to the bottom bun. Place the rested, Gruyère-melted patty on the greens. Spoon a generous amount of caramelized onions over the patty. Carefully place one Swiss cheese crisp on top of the onions — it should extend slightly beyond the patty, proud and architectural. Add a pinch of flaky salt. Close with the top bun gently so as not to shatter the crisp completely — some fracturing is inevitable and desirable. Serve immediately.
